27074:
Joshua son of Nun, an Ephraimite, grew from Moses' young aide and field commander into his successor. With Caleb he alone among the twelve spies urged Israel to trust God and enter Canaan, and so only they of the exodus generation survived to do it. Commissioned by the laying on of Moses' hands, he led Israel across the Jordan, took Jericho, Ai and Hazor, and divided the land among the tribes. He ended his life calling Israel to renew the covenant at Shechem.

The Book of Joshua portrays him as a second Moses. Waters part before him, he removes his sandals on holy ground, he mediates the covenant, and he is repeatedly called to meditate on the law and be strong and courageous. He is not flawless: he attacks Ai without seeking God and is tricked by the Gibeonites because he 'asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD' (Josh 9:14). But the book ends with the note that Israel served the LORD all his days.

The conquest raises two large debates. The first is historical. Excavations at Jericho, Ai and Hazor are read in different ways, and many scholars favour gradual settlement or peasant-revolt models over a swift campaign; the text itself also notes much land left unconquered (Josh 13:1). The second is ethical: how to understand the command to devote Canaanite cities to destruction. Christians have also seen in his name, the Hebrew form of Jesus, a foreshadowing of the one who leads God's people into rest.
27075: The text says he was the son of Nun of Ephraim, first named Hoshea. He fought Amalek, served Moses, spied out Canaan and gave a faithful report, and was commissioned with Moses' hands laid on him. He led the crossing of the Jordan and the wars of Joshua 6–12, allotted the land, and renewed the covenant at Shechem. He died at 110 and was buried at Timnath-serah in Ephraim. Joshua 10 says the sun stood still at his word, and Joshua 11:23 says he took 'the whole land', although Joshua 13:1 and Judges 1 list territory left unconquered.
27076: Joshua is the faithful disciple who received the Torah from Moses and passed it to the elders, the second link in the chain of tradition (*Avot* 1:1). The rabbis remember him as the student who never left the tent. Rabbinic tradition also credits him with writing the book of Joshua (b. Bava Batra 15a).
27077: The Fathers read Joshua as a type of Jesus. The two share a name, and Joshua, not Moses (the law), brings the people into the promised land. The Jordan crossing prefigures baptism and Rahab's scarlet cord prefigures redemption by blood (Origen, *Homilies on Joshua*).
27078: Joshua shows covenant faithfulness and God keeping his promises to Abraham. The conquest is read as a unique, limited act of divine judgment on Canaanite sin (Gen 15:16), not a model for later warfare. Hebrews 4:8 shows that Joshua's rest was a foretaste of a greater Sabbath rest.
27080: Most historians see the conquest account as a later theological narrative, edited within the Deuteronomistic History. It compresses a long and complex emergence of Israel in the highlands. Others, notably some evangelical archaeologists, argue for a historical core and point to the burning of Hazor and, under early dating, to the walls of Jericho.

27092: Late Bronze Age Canaan was a patchwork of city-states under Egyptian overlordship. The Amarna letters (c. 1350 BC) show local kings complaining about raiders called 'Habiru'; some link the Habiru with Hebrews, though most scholars think the terms are not equivalent. Hazor was the largest city in the region, and its Late Bronze city was destroyed by fire. Early Iron Age villages spread across the central hill country in the 12th–11th centuries BC. 'Devoting' a city to a god (herem) is also known from Moab's Mesha Stele.
27093: Joshua's charge, 'Be strong and of a good courage', and his choice, 'as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD', are among the most quoted lines in Scripture. The conquest narrative was used across history to justify Christian crusades and colonial wars, and modern ethics and theology are still working through that misuse. Christians read him as a figure of Jesus who brings God's people into their inheritance.

27096: Joshua married Rahab, and prophets and priests descended from them.

27212: Phinehas, grandson of Aaron, is remembered for his violent zeal at Baal-peor, which Psalm 106 says was 'counted unto him for righteousness'.
